title: Fake eBay Ad in Google Search Results Leads to Tech Support Scam
description: An advertising campaign pretending to be eBay has been discovered in the Google search results that leads to a Tech Support Scam.

Typically you have to find the ad let's see and there we go, right here, we have the eBay official site. Notice that it has a www.ebay.com link when we click on it though. It redirect us Your computer has been locked up. Your IP address was used without your knowledge or consent to visit website that contains, identity of theft virus to unlock the computer please call support immediately please this bad ad campaign was shared with bleeping computer by a researcher who wants to remain anonymous he has reported to Google and hopefully they'll take care of the security lost there because even if it has to be really mean how do you blame you up stuck with this tech support skin

textual.observation: An advertising campaign presented as eBay in Google search results is described as redirecting users to a different site associated with a tech support scam.

evidence.quote: An advertising campaign pretending to be eBay has been discovered in the Google search results that leads to a Tech Support Scam.
it will redirect you instead to a different site other than eBay which redirects you to a tech support scam

textual.context: Presented as the subject of an explanatory video discussing a bad advertisement; the source does not establish whether the campaign is currently active.
textual.potential_relevance: The stated eBay identity and search-result placement are linked to a destination described as different from eBay and associated with a tech support scam, making the identity-to-destination relationship relevant for later review.
textual.limitations: These records do not independently verify the advertisement, the destination, the affiliation claim, or any user outcome.

textual.observation: The described destination displays a message claiming that the viewer's computer is locked and instructing the viewer to call support immediately.

evidence.quote: Your computer has been locked up. Your IP address was used without your knowledge or consent to visit website that contains, identity of theft virus to unlock the computer please call support immediately

textual.context: Quoted as on-screen content encountered after the redirect in the video's demonstration or discussion; the ASR contains transcription errors, including in the wording of the alleged warning.
textual.potential_relevance: A claimed computer problem and alleged virus are directly linked to an urgent instruction to call support, which is a concretely described support-contact mechanism requiring later context assessment.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish whether the computer was actually locked, whether a virus was present, who would receive the call, or whether any payment or data request followed.

visual.observation: A browser page displays a prominent “VIRUS ALERT FROM MICROSOFT” message claiming that the computer is blocked, while directing the viewer to call “[PHONE]” and showing a matching “Contact Us” button.
visual.context: Visible on-screen alert and support-style page; the sampled frames do not establish whether this is a warning, demonstration, or live support interaction.
visual.potential_relevance: A claimed Microsoft security identity is directly linked to an urgent request to contact a displayed phone number, which is a concrete support-alert relationship for review.
visual.limitations: The frames cannot establish who controls the page, whether the phone number connects to anyone, or whether any viewer contacted it.

visual.observation: The same alert says “Enter Windows registration key to unblock” and provides an input field with a “Submit” button, alongside statements that the computer is blocked and that information may be extracted if the user closes the page.
visual.context: The request appears inside a browser popup styled as a Microsoft virus/security alert, with a separate “Close to ignore” button.
visual.potential_relevance: The claimed security problem is tied to a request to submit a Windows registration key in order to unblock the computer, creating a specific sensitive-input and access-condition relationship.
visual.limitations: The sampled frames cannot establish whether any key was entered, submitted, collected, or used, nor whether the alert’s claims were accurate.

textual_context_notes.observation: The source frames the content as an examination of a bad advertisement rather than an endorsement of it.

evidence.quote: In this video we take a look at a bad ad that's appearing in the google search result pages.

textual_context_notes.observation: The described campaign was reportedly shared with a publication by an anonymous researcher and reported to Google.

visual_context_notes.observation: The browser address bar visibly shows a non-Microsoft-looking domain while the page uses Microsoft-related branding and labels such as “VIRUS ALERT FROM MICROSOFT” and “Microsoft Security Alert.”

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it examines and reports a problematic search advertisement rather than presenting it as the creator’s own offer. The eBay search result, false virus-alert page, and requests for a support call and Windows registration key are depicted as subjects of the investigation, and the creator is not shown soliciting payment, credentials, or participation.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary theme is an investigation and report of a deceptive search advertisement and a support-alert flow, rather than promotion of that flow by the video creator.
